- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is low (≤0.3) or negative, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for risk aversion or market panic.
- Model consistently overreacts to recent spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days) — cap forecast rise to 2–4% after a spike, then allow gradual mean reversion.
- If 3+ consecutive days of high sentiment + rising prices, model tends to overshoot; apply downward correction of 2–5% in next 3–5 days.
- Model underestimates when sentiment is volatile or mixed (0.3–0.7) — adjust upward by 1–2% if sentiment is trending upward.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, model often fails to capture mean reversion — if recent 7–14 day average is above 30d average, reduce forecast by 1–3% to align with historical mean.
- If sentiment is consistently 1.0 (strong bullish) and price is rising, model may overfit — reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- If sentiment is 0.0–0.2 (bearish) and price is falling, model may underfit — increase forecast by 1–2% to account for hidden support or reversal.
